Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
I try to erase the memory of the event

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
The world is a dangerous place
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 78-year-old woman whose index trauma is a natural disaster, this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, appraisals, memory items, and strategies all fit disaster-related loss/danger themes, but 'being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/sexual-trauma context that is not represented anywhere else in the formulation or item set. This is more than unusual; it introduces a qualitatively different trauma meaning network without supporting items in Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategies.

vignette:
Eleanor was seventy-eight when the Marshall Fire tore through her Colorado neighborhood, devouring everything in its path. She and her husband Robert had twenty minutes to grab their go-bag and their elderly cat, but the cat panicked and ran under the bed; by the time Eleanor coaxed her out, the smoke was so thick she couldn't see. They made it to the car, but Eleanor's childhood friend Margaret, who lived two doors down, turned back for her dog and never came out. The fire was later ruled an accident-a downed power line-and the utility company paid a fine but admitted no fault. The official report used words like "unprecedented" and "act of God," and Eleanor felt the bottom drop out of her understanding of fairness.

In the months afterward, Eleanor tried to return to her freelance graphic design work from a temporary apartment, but the world felt unrecognizable. She had always believed that if you worked hard and were good to people, life would be fair; that belief was gone now, replaced by a quiet certainty that the world was actively dangerous and that what happened to her was deeply unjust and no one had done anything about it. And it was precisely this conviction-that the world was now unpredictable and malevolent-that kept pulling her back into the fire's memory, as if she needed to re-play it to confirm she hadn't imagined its cruelty. This conviction seeped into everything. Once she saw the world as fundamentally unsafe, ordinary moments she would once have ignored-a car backfiring, the hum of a distant siren-now snagged her attention, each one a fresh confirmation that danger was always near. When a door slammed in the apartment hallway, her heart seized-the sound seemed to confirm that danger could come from anywhere, at any moment, without warning. The same happened when she caught a whiff of alcohol; a neighbor's beer at a barbecue made her stomach knot because she smelled it on the man who had refused to evacuate, laughing and drinking on his porch while the fire crested the ridge. And when a friend at the senior center talked about her son's recent loss of a spouse, Eleanor had to excuse herself-she couldn't bear to hear the words "lost" or "gone," because they yanked her back into the belief that the world was not just dangerous but pointlessly cruel.

She began cleaning. Every morning, she scrubbed the kitchen counters until they gleamed; she reorganized the pantry by height and then by color; she dusted the same shelf three times in an hour. The compulsive organizing gave her a fragile sense of control, a small rebellion against the chaos that had swallowed her life. She also caught herself dwelling, endlessly looped, on how the fire could have been prevented: if the power company had trimmed the trees, if the evacuation order had come earlier, if she had grabbed the cat sooner. The rumination felt like a kind of mental labor, as though she could undo the event by sheer force of thought. And when the images became unbearable, she tried to erase the memory entirely-she would put on loud music, scrub a spot on the floor, will herself to stop seeing Margaret's face at the door.

But the memory fought back. Sometimes Eleanor could narrate the event in a flat, detached voice, as if it happened to a stranger, and that numbness frightened her more than the panic. At other moments, the memory roared in and felt as present as the room around her-she would be slicing vegetables and suddenly be back in the smoky driveway, the heat on her skin, the cat yowling. The extreme nature of it all made the story feel almost unreal, as though it couldn't have happened to her, even as the flashback pinned her in place. She tried harder to push it away, but the more she cleaned and ruminated, the more the memory intruded. The cleaning became a trigger itself: each time she dusted a picture frame, she saw the room that once held it, and the door-slam of a cabinet would send her spiraling into the belief that she was never safe. She felt trapped in a cycle where her own strategies to cope only sharpened the very triggers and memories she was trying to escape.

Three years later, Eleanor still works as a graphic designer, but she has stopped taking jobs that involve meeting clients in their homes-the unfamiliar doors, the sudden slams. She works exclusively from her new house, which she has arranged in rigid order, and she avoids the news about natural disasters entirely. Last week, her husband gently asked if she wanted to attend a memorial for Margaret. The question sent her into a three-day cleaning binge that left her hands raw. She finally called a therapist because she was terrified that she would never feel safe again, and because, despite all her efforts, the memory of the fire still felt more real than anything in her current life.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not contain a causal link where negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs that the world is dangerous or unjust) lead to the intrusion of the traumatic memory; instead, memory intrudes independently or is triggered by external cues.

The vignette shows triggers leading to negative appraisals, but not the reverse: negative appraisals causing or creating new triggers; it does not convey that the appraisal itself generates the triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not contain a causal link where negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs that the world is dangerous or unjust) lead to the intrusion of the traumatic memory; instead, memory intrudes independently or is triggered by external cues.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette shows triggers leading to negative appraisals, but not the reverse: negative appraisals causing or creating new triggers; it does not convey that the appraisal itself generates the triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
